evidence_items.excerpt: Commit message: [Fiber] Detect useSyncExternalStore mutations missed while Activity tree was hidden (#36947) Fixes #27670. When an Activity subtree is hidden, its passive effects are disconnected, which unsubscribes from the store. On reveal, the effects are reconnected by replaying the fiber's effect list without a render, but if `updateStoreInstance` was not in the effect list then the component would be left stale. This happened both when a layout effect mutated the store during the reveal commit (after the subtree rendered but before it resubscribed) and when the store changed while hidden and the component bailed out of rendering during the reveal. We now push the updateStoreInstance effect unconditionally but tag it with HookHasEffect only under the same conditions as before, so regular commits skip it when nothing changed but reconnection always triggers it so it can trigger a rerender if appropriate. evidence_items.excerpt: Commit message: [Fizz] Extend stack overflow recovery to retries (#36977) Ran into this test failure as part of https://github.com/react/react/pull/36917 - it seems that the added code was just enough to increase stack size and fail the deep tree recovery test in CI. Looking into that, there appears to be a gap here with retries, including a TODO test case for the scenario. Fizz recovers from stack overflows in extremely deep trees by catching the first overflow in the `renderNode` trampoline and spawning a continuation task. That continuation is retried via `retryRenderTask → retryNode`, which has no trampoline above it. So if the remaining tree still doesn't fit in one fresh stack, the overflow was treated as a fatal error instead of recovering again. This fix re-schedules the task when a retried render overflows but `task.node` advanced (proving forward progress was made). If this is a real in-component overflow, `task.node` doesn't advance and we still fail. The existing test used `n={1000}`, which only required one recovery round and didn't catch this gap in source mode. It's updated to `n={1200}`, which reliably requires multiple recovery rounds. evidence_items.excerpt: Issue title: With Node.js now offering solid support for require(esm), I suggest React consider a pure ESM build for its next major release. State: OPEN With Node.js now offering solid support for require(esm), I suggest React consider a pure ESM build for its next major release. Currently, React’s primary build artifacts published to npm are still based on CommonJS. Historically, retaining CommonJS made practical sense for compatibility, as a vast number of Node.js tooling and server-side applications rely on synchronous `require()` to load React. But today, newer versions of Node.js can synchronously load ESM modules via `require()`, the fundamental blocker preventing React from migrating to a pure ESM build has essentially disappeared. Therefore, I believe a pure ESM build for React is now practically viable in the next major version, and I encourage the React team to evaluate this direction. Given that a new major release would likely bump the minimum Node.js runtime requirement as well, this might be the perfect timing to push forward with a pure ESM build.

evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: I investigated this on the current checkout and I think the observed delay is caused by the interaction between `React.lazy` initialization and Suspense retry throttling, rather than `React.lazy` synchronously knowing that the preloaded native Promise has already fulfilled. In the repro, the loader is called outside React before the click, so the native Promise resolves, but the `React.lazy` payload itself is still `Uninitialized` until the lazy component is first rendered. On that first render, `React.lazy` calls the loader and receives an already-fulfilled native Promise, but native Promises do not expose synchronous fulfilled state. React attaches `.then()`, the callback runs in a later microtask, and the lazy payload is marked `Pending`/throws the thenable for that render. The ~300ms delay appears to come from Suspense retry throttling rather than from `React.lazy` itself: - `packages/react/src/ReactLazy.js` initializes the lazy payload only when React renders the lazy type. - `packages/react/src/ReactLazy.js` cannot synchronously unwrap an already-fulfilled native Promise. - `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` uses `FALLBACK_THROTTLE_MS = 300`…

evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: I investigated the compiler pipeline and traced the memoization loss back to reactive scope construction and mutable-range analysis. The callback itself isn't special, and the memoization drop occurs after `FlattenScopesWithHooksOrUseHIR` prunes a scope that spans `getIsChromatic()`, `useResizeDetector()`, the callback, and the `classnames(..., { isChromatic })` path. The interesting part is that `getIsChromatic()` is treated as `ValueKind.Mutable` because it has no known function signature. That causes alias propagation and mutable-range expansion through the object literal passed to `classnames`, which eventually places the callback and classnames path into the same reactive scope. The resulting scope crosses the hook boundary and is pruned, which removes callback memoization. I also found existing compiler tests and comments describing similar mutable-range entanglement cases as a known limitation, including a fixture comment stating: > "This function should be memoized, but its mutable range is entangled with the useContext call..." evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: Thanks for the clarification — I agree that this is counterintuitive. The compiler currently treats the function identities themselves as the safe memoization boundary. In your example, it can’t assume that "cheapFunction()" is independent of "cheapFunction"’s identity, so when that identity changes it conservatively recomputes the whole expression. The "useMemo" version gives the compiler an explicit boundary, which is why it can split the work into two memoized steps. So yes, removing "useMemo" can change the generated memoization strategy today, and that’s a limitation of the compiler rather than something you should have to reason about from the output in every case. If you have a reduced repro where the compiler is missing an optimization it should preserve, please share it — otherwise the safest guidance for now is to keep the explicit memoization where that boundary matters. evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: Opened a fix for this in #36857. Root cause: `isChromatic` is created before the `useResizeDetector()` hook, then read by the `ref` callback and also captured by the `className` expression. Its reactive scope ends up spanning the hook call, and since scopes can't span hooks they're pruned wholesale — so the ref callback never memoizes and gets a fresh identity every render (the detach/reattach you're seeing). The PR makes hook/`use()` calls act as reactive-scope barriers so the ref callback memoizes independently. Added a regression fixture based on your repro; full compiler fixture suite passes with no regressions.

evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: I have identified the root cause and prepared a fix. ## Root Cause `binaryToComparableString` uses `String.fromCharCode.apply(String, largeArray)`, which passes each byte as a separate argument. evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: ﻿Hey @JHON12091986, thanks for digging into this. Your root-cause analysis is correct: the crash comes from `String.fromCharCode.apply` spreading every byte as a separate argument and exceeding the engine argument limit. On some engines (historically JavaScriptCore/Safari) that cap is around 65536 or lower, so a chunk of exactly 65536 can still throw the same `RangeError`. The `if (uint8.length <= 65536)` fast path has the same risk. A safer, conventional value is `0x8000` (32768). Minor: `uint8.subarray(...)` is a zero-copy view, while `.slice(...)` copies each chunk. evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: @eps1lon could you take a look when you get a chance? Quick summary of what this fixes and what I verified: - Path 2 of #37014: a concurrent client update was unconditionally discarding a dehydrated boundary even when it was already \`$~\` (queued for reveal, content already streamed) — racing the reveal and causing the transient duplication. - Fix: treat \`$~\` like the existing "still pending" case (bail, keep dehydrated content) instead of falling through to \`retrySuspenseComponentWithoutHydrating\`. - Verified two ways: (1) a deterministic unit test that fails without the change and passes with it, and (2) manual testing against a real Next.js App Router production build (patched React linked in), where the race was reproduced live in a browser with no duplication/errors. Thanks in advance!

File went from about 2300 lines to about 1320 lines with no behavior change intended (verified with `yarn snap minimize` against a hand built fixture). However, when the children of this filtered suspense boundary are later reordered, the backend agent was still pushing a `SUSPENSE_TREE_OPERATION_REORDER_CHILDREN` operation containing the ID of the filtered node (coerced/cast as `0` since it has a `FilteredFiberInstance` kind). This caused the frontend `Store` to attempt to resolve node `0` from `_idToSuspense`, resulting in the `Cannot reorder children for suspense node "0" because no matching node was found in the Store` crash. ### Solution 1. Added an early return to `recordResetSuspenseChildren` in `packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/fiber/renderer.js` if the parent instance is filtered (i.e. `kind !== FIBER_INSTANCE`), matching the early return behavior in `recordSuspenseResize` and `recordSuspenseSuspenders`. 2. evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: After exploring some of the compiler source I realized this is probably intended behavior. It all got a bit technical, but I think the shortest explanation that is easy to understand is: Given the component props: ```ts { nodes: [], selection: { node: null }, } ``` The callback `n => n.id === selection?.node.id` would never run, ensuring the invalid access of `node.id` would not throw an error. React compiler code may not alter this behavior; if it were to try and access `id` even when `nodes.length === 0`, the compiled component would now throw. Adding the unconditional evaluation of `selection?.node.id` makes the component throw regardless of the compiler check. That sounds bad, but it means the compiler is now free to depend on that same read; if it fails it wouldn't make a difference. In my example, I typed `selection.node` to be non-nullable. I failed to realize the compiler does not and should not rely on static types. --- I'm not sure if I should close this issue, or if it maybe should be a feature request? Seeing that the compiler code knows exactly what's going on, it feels like we can also make it understand when the callback passed to `find` runs?

evidence_items.excerpt: Issue comment: **Reproduced, and the proposed fix verified.** **Environment:** macOS (Darwin 25.2.0), Node.js v26.0.0, `react@19.2.8`, `react-dom@19.2.8`, `jsdom@29.1.1` The crash reproduces deterministically with a minimal script — concurrent render via `createRoot`, then deleting `global.window` / `global.document` before the deferred Scheduler task fires: ``` ReferenceError: window is not defined at performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask (react-dom-client.development.js) at Immediate.performWorkUntilDeadline (scheduler.development.js) ``` I also verified the fix empirically: applying the guard ```js typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.event : undefined ``` to the three unguarded reads (`trackSchedulerEvent`, `resolveEventType`, `resolveEventTimeStamp`) in the development bundle makes the exact same repro exit cleanly, with the scheduled task completing safely. This matches the change proposed in #37102. I also ran the identical script against `react@19.1.1` / `react-dom@19.1.1` and can confirm it does not crash there, consistent with this being a 19.2.0 regression.

Numeric keys are meant to sort before non-numeric keys. The bug: when a non-numeric key was compared against a numeric key, the function fell through to a plain string comparison. Keys that start with a character below "0" (like "$ref" or "#id") were placed before numeric keys instead of after them. The comparison could also disagree with itself depending on argument order, so the list could end up inconsistently ordered. The fix returns 1 when the other key is numeric, so numeric keys always sort first, matching the existing numeric branch. I also added unit tests for alphaSortEntries.

Each node has previous and awaited fields that form strong-reference linked lists pointing back through the ancestry chain. The bug: When destroy(asyncId) fires, only the map entry is removed — but the node object itself stays alive because newer nodes reference it via their previous/awaited fields.
